source.title: Small Data? No Problem! Exploring the Viability of Pretrained Multilingual Language Models for Low-resourced Languages
source.authors: Kelechi Ogueji; Yu-Xin Zhu; Jimmy Lin

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses and cites Kaplan et al.'s scaling findings, but does not test the stated loss power laws, extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation. Its architecture experiments report downstream NER scores rather than held-out pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: The paper reports architecture-variant NER results, recorded below as findings about downstream performance rather than as tests of the claim versions. Its held-out perplexity evaluation is described, but no scaling results for that measure are reported. Kaplan et al.'s findings are cited, not tested.
record.test_reason: The paper cites Kaplan et al. (2020) to interpret its depth results, but reports no held-out loss scaling, no power-law fits, no extrapolation and no compute-optimal allocation. Its design-space sweeps (Tables 4–6) use downstream NER dev F1 to choose a final architecture. The pretraining perplexity it evaluates is never reported. No version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The main conclusion is that competitive multilingual MLMs can be pretrained from scratch on under 1 GB of data in low-resource African languages, with no high-resource transfer. AfriBERTa matches or beats mBERT and XLM-R on several languages. The design-space findings are secondary: deeper models are better with diminishing gains, deep models need few heads, and larger vocabularies are not always better.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains multilingual masked-language models on a small African-language corpus and compares architecture variants using downstream NER and classification. It does not reproduce a scaling-law loss sweep or compute-optimal allocation procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported downstream NER results vary with layer depth, number of attention heads, and vocabulary size.

fits_no_version.finding: At roughly fixed parameter count (about 74.5M), going from 4 to 10 layers changes average NER dev F1 only from 75.97 to 77.27. Gains diminish with depth.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream analogue of V4: at fixed parameter count, depth changes downstream fine-tuning performance only modestly in small-data multilingual MLMs.

fits_no_version.finding: Attention-head count and vocabulary size (25k–85k) change average NER F1 by up to about 1.5 points. Vocabulary effects are non-monotonic: 70k is best, 85k is worse.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In small-data multilingual MLMs, vocabulary size and head count have non-monotonic, small effects on downstream NER performance.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 1st Workshop on Multilingual Representation Learning
record.problems: The architecture comparisons report downstream NER F1 rather than held-out pretraining loss. Scores are averages over three seeds, but no error bars or other uncertainty measures are given. The study does not run parameter/token/compute scaling or allocation experiments.

untested.parts: No held-out loss is reported against parameters, tokens or compute. Perplexity is evaluated but not reported.
No small-run fit is used to predict larger runs.
There is no fixed-compute sweep over parameters and tokens.
The fixed-parameter depth sweep (Table 4) is measured by NER F1, not pretraining loss.
The study uses text MLM pretraining only. Other modalities and regimes are not studied.
NER F1 is reported for a few model sizes (Tables 5 and 7), but no scale trend or loss–downstream relation is fitted or tested. Size is also confounded with depth and vocabulary.
No exponents or fitting choices are examined.

record.verdict_notes: All rows are design-space selection runs scored by NER dev F1, so linking them to 'none' is correct. T6-vocab-40k is the same configuration and value (78.09) as T5-8L-6H. The final models in Table 7 (small 97M, base 111M, large 126M) score 76.20, 78.60 and 79.10 average test F1. This is downstream performance rising with size, but the sizes are confounded with depth and there are only three points, so it is not a V6 test. The authors' reading that Kaplan et al. explain the diminishing depth gains is a loose interpretation, not a test.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law relationship between held-out loss and parameters, tokens, or compute is measured.
No small-run fits or large-run loss predictions are evaluated.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or parameter/token growth trend is measured.
Architecture variants are compared using downstream NER F1, not held-out pretraining loss.
The study concerns multilingual text pretraining and does not test other modalities or the listed training regimes.
Downstream tasks are evaluated, but the paper does not test whether their performance improves predictably with scale or pretraining loss.
No power-law exponents, fitting choices, or curve bending are investigated.
